passage:
Manoj and I have been together since the school trip to Mysuru, five months now. Looking back, what surprises me is how easy it feels.
On Saturdays I play football with my old group, and Manoj goes to his drawing class. Neither of us sulks about it. Last week he asked if I wanted to skip football for a film. I said no, the match mattered to me. He just said, "Okay, next Saturday then," and that was the end of it.
When I asked if I could hold his hand at the fair, he said, "Not in front of my cousins, maybe later." I said sure. It didn't feel like a rejection, just a real answer.
We talk about everything, even the awkward stuff. I think that's why it keeps growing. Nobody owns anybody. I'm Kiran, I'm fifteen, and this is the first time liking someone has felt calm.

qa.q: Where did Kiran and Manoj get together?
qa.a: On the school trip to Mysuru.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about the relationship?
qa.a: Kiran feels calm and happy, affectionate towards Manoj without fear, because either of them can say no.

qa.q: What habits help their relationship grow?
qa.a: Keeping their own friends and interests, talking openly, and accepting each other's no each time, like at the fair.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Kiran's easy acceptance at the fair?
qa.a: Manoj probably feels respected and relaxed, knowing he can set a limit without Kiran getting upset.

grounding: A teen in a relationship where both can say no, keep their friends and talk openly feels calm, respectful affection.

Class teacher's observation, Class 12B, Friday
I have noticed Vijay and Aadhya are going out; most of the class knows. I'm recording this because it's a good example, not a concern.
This week the class planned a Saturday trip to the lake. Aadhya said she'd stay back for her physics study group. Vijay looked disappointed for a second, then said, "Fair. Send me the notes after?" and went with his friends. Neither made a scene.
On Wednesday, in the corridor, I heard Vijay ask, "Is it okay if I sit with you at lunch, or are you with the girls today?" Aadhya said, "With the girls today." He smiled and joined the cricket boys.
They each still have their own friends. They check with each other rather than assume.
No action needed. I will, with their permission, ask them to help me plan the life-skills session on healthy friendships and relationships next month.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya stay back from the lake trip?
qa.a: For her physics study group.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when Aadhya said she would stay back?
qa.a: He felt a moment of disappointment but accepted her choice calmly, showing respect rather than hurt pride.

qa.q: What does this couple do that keeps the relationship healthy?
qa.a: They ask instead of assuming, accept each other's no without a scene, and keep their own friends.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Vijay accepts her choices?
qa.a: Aadhya likely feels trusted and free, able to say no without worrying about upsetting Vijay.

grounding: A teacher observes a teen couple who both can say no, keep their friends and check with each other, a picture of respectful affection.

"Come on, Swati. Everyone kisses in the park. Everyone."
"Rishabh, I said I'm not ready."
"You're being so childish. My friends' girlfriends don't make such a fuss."
"Then maybe you should go out with them."
"That's not what I mean. I just thought you liked me."
"I do like you. And I'm still saying no."
He kicked a stone. "Whatever." He walked off towards the gate.
That evening, Swati sat on Vandana's balcony, hugging her knees.
"Maybe I should've just done it. So he doesn't leave."
Vandana shook her head. "Swati. You said no. That's a full sentence."
"He said everyone does it."
"Everyone doesn't. And even if they did, so what? Someone who actually respects you would say 'okay' and mean it."
Swati was quiet for a long time. "He didn't say okay."
"No," Vandana said gently. "He didn't."

qa.a: In the park.

passage:
Last winter, my boyfriend Sahir wanted me to sneak out at night for his friend's party. There would be drinks, older boys, no adults. "Everyone goes, Avni," he kept saying. "You'll look like a baby if you don't."
I didn't want to go. It wasn't about being a good girl. I just wasn't ready, and it didn't feel safe.
He sent me twenty messages that week. Some were sweet, some were angry. The pressure made my head spin. My friend Uma saw me checking my phone in class and asked what was wrong. When I told her, she said simply, "No is a complete answer, Avni."
That night I told Sahir: "No. Not going. Final." He called me boring and didn't talk to me for three days. I almost gave in. I didn't.
We broke up a month later. I don't regret it. Someone who respected me would have heard my no the first time.

qa.q: How many messages did Sahir send Avni that week?
qa.a: Twenty messages.

qa.q: How did Avni feel during the week of pressure?
qa.a: She felt anxious and dizzy with pressure, confused by Sahir's sweet and angry messages, and almost gave in.

qa.q: Which choice was wise, and why?
qa.a: Avni gave a clear, final no and held to it, even when he sulked, because a respectful partner accepts no.

qa.q: How might Uma see Avni's situation?
qa.a: Uma seems worried and protective, reminding Avni plainly that her no is enough.

grounding: A teen pressed by her boyfriend to sneak out to a party says no and holds to it, recognising that a respectful partner would accept it.

School counsellor's note, Monday
Uma came to see me on her own after the morning assembly. She said she had "done something ugly" in her relationship with Divyansh.
Over the weekend he had gone to his cousin's wedding instead of her dance recital. She didn't reply to his messages for two days, on purpose. When he called, she said, "Fine, I guess I'm not important." She admitted she knew it would make him feel guilty, and that she had done it before.
She said, "My sister calls it passion, but it feels like a trick." I told her that noticing the pattern was the hard part, and asked what she wanted instead. She said, "To just say, 'I was hurt you missed it.'"
We practised saying it aloud. She planned to apologise to Divyansh at lunch today and ask him directly next time. I will check in with her on Friday to see how it went.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh miss Uma's dance recital?
qa.a: He went to his cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she came to the counsellor?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, calling her silent treatment 'ugly' and a trick she had used before.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor help Uma take?
qa.a: Noticing the pattern, apologising to Divyansh, and practising a direct way to say she was hurt instead of using silence or guilt.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt during Uma's two days of silence?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt anxious and guilty, confused about what he had done and under pressure to make it up to her.

grounding: A teen notices she uses silent treatment and guilt to get her way, apologises, and learns to ask directly instead.

Hemant had to cancel our evening walk because his Nana is in hospital. I knew that. I still wrote, "Wow, okay. Guess I know where I stand." Then I didn't reply to anything he said for hours.
I watched him type, stop, type again. Some part of me, the part Didi calls my drama-queen side, liked it. Like I was winning something.

Tomorrow I'll tell him, "I'm sorry. That was unfair. I hope your Nana gets better." And next time I'm disappointed, I'll just say, "I'm disappointed, can we plan another day?" Directly. No games.

The breakup with Aparna happened on Sunday at the village tank, in four sentences. By Wednesday Kiran felt empty, as if someone had scooped out his chest.
He replayed it all day: her face, the way she said "I'm sorry," what he should have said instead. At night he lay on the charpai on the roof, phone in hand, typing messages to her and deleting them. He watched videos until two in the morning just to stop thinking.
On Thursday his friend Bhola found him skipping lunch behind the school pump. "You look like a ghost," Bhola said. He dragged Kiran home to eat his mother's kadhi.
That night, Kiran put his phone downstairs before bed. He made himself eat breakfast. On Saturday, he went to cricket with Bhola's brothers even though he didn't feel like it.
It still hurt. But he wasn't going to message her. He was just going to let it hurt, and wait.

qa.q: Where did Kiran and Aparna break up?
qa.a: At the village tank.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel in the days after the breakup?
qa.a: He felt hollow and empty, replaying the breakup constantly and struggling to stop thinking about it.

qa.q: Which choices helped Kiran cope?
qa.a: Eating with Bhola's family, putting his phone downstairs at night, keeping breakfast and cricket, and not messaging Aparna.

qa.q: How does Bhola see Kiran after the breakup?
qa.a: Bhola is worried, seeing Kiran looking like a ghost, and takes him home to eat so he is not alone.

passage:
Two weeks after Lukas ended it, Astrid still felt like a hollow shell walking around Oslo. She replayed their last conversation on the bus, in the shower, in maths. What if she'd said something different?
Every night she opened a message to him. "Can we just talk once more?" She never sent it, but she read it over and over, then scrolled through videos until three.
Her friend Ada noticed the dark circles. On Friday she showed up at Astrid's door with a bag of cinnamon buns. "You're not okay. That's allowed," she said.
They made a plan together on Astrid's bed: phone charging in the hall at night, dinner with the family even if she wasn't hungry, skating with Ada every Sunday.
"It's going to hurt for a while," Ada said.
"I know," Astrid said, and cried properly for the first time, which, strangely, helped.

qa.q: What did Ada bring when she showed up?
qa.a: A bag of cinnamon buns.

qa.q: How was Astrid feeling in the two weeks after the breakup?
qa.a: She felt hollow and stuck, replaying their last talk and longing to message Lukas.

qa.q: What small steps did Ada and Astrid plan, and why do they help?
qa.a: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom, eating family dinners and skating on Sundays protect sleep, food and friendship while the hurt heals.

qa.a: Ada sees it as normal and allowed, and she wants to support her friend with company rather than push her to be fine.

passage:
Afreen, you're angry at him. Good. Anger means you cared. But listen to what I did at your age.
When I was sixteen, in Kanpur, Shaheen broke up with me by a note in my geography book. Two days later she was laughing with another boy by the canteen. I was so furious I shook. I had photos of us, and her messages. I sat with my finger on the button, ready to send them to the whole class. I wanted her to feel what I felt.
The turning point was my cousin Irfan. He took the phone out of my hand and said, "If you send that, you become the story. Not her."
So instead I wrote five pages in a notebook, every angry word. Then I ran around the colony ground until I couldn't breathe. That night, I told Irfan everything, again and again.
I never sent anything. Your Naveen Chacha's proudest moment, that.

qa.a: His cousin Irfan took the phone away; Naveen then wrote out his anger, ran around the colony ground and talked to Irfan.

It was board exam week, and Dilnaz still had to sit through tuition with Madhav, who'd broken up with her by text on Monday and then posted a photo with his new group on Wednesday, grinning.
She was so angry her pen tore the page. At home she opened their old chat. There was one photo of him in his school play costume, looking ridiculous. Posting it would take one second. He deserved it.

She shut the phone in her drawer, pulled out her rough notebook and wrote in big furious letters: I HATE THAT YOU MADE ME FEEL STUPID. She filled three pages.
Then she skipped rope on the terrace until her calves burned.
At night she called her friend Nargis and ranted for twenty minutes. Nargis just listened. The next morning, Dilnaz sat for her chemistry paper and didn't once look at his account.

Valeria broke up with Santiago on a Tuesday, outside the bakery near their school in Seville. "I just don't feel it anymore," she said, and walked away.
For days, Santiago felt worthless. He looked in the mirror and saw only reasons: too quiet, too thin, too boring. At night he drafted messages: I'll change. Just tell me what to do. Give me one more chance.
His friend Emeka found him sitting on the steps after football practice, staring at the phone.
"You're going to beg, aren't you."
"Maybe."
"Tell me three things wrong with you."
Santiago listed them.
Emeka shook his head. "She stopped feeling it. That's about her feelings, not a list of your faults. You're still the guy who scored twice today."
Santiago deleted the draft. He came to Emeka's house for dinner that weekend and the next. It still hurt, but he stopped writing the list.

qa.a: Outside the bakery near their school in Seville.

qa.q: How did Santiago feel about himself after the breakup?
qa.a: He felt worthless, looking in the mirror and listing everything wrong with himself.

qa.q: What helped Santiago avoid begging?
qa.a: Emeka challenged his list of faults, reminded him the breakup was about Valeria's feelings, and kept him close with dinners.

grounding: A teen dumped by his girlfriend feels worthless, is tempted to beg, and with a friend's help sees it says nothing about his value.

The girls' hostel lights went off at ten, but Gopika sat in the corridor with her phone glowing. Harish had ended it that afternoon by the college bus stop: "It's not working. Sorry."
She'd already written him six messages. Please. I'll be better. What did I do? She hadn't sent them. Yet.
In her notebook she'd written, I'm not good enough for anyone.

Mrs Iyer read the line and shook her head. "A breakup tells you something about two people together. It doesn't tell you your worth."
She walked Gopika back to her room and asked her roommate Leena to keep her company. "Come to my office tomorrow after class," she added. "We'll talk again." Gopika deleted the six drafts before sleeping.

passage:
Okay, Kevin, you asked, so here's the honest version. I'm Joseph, and three months ago I broke up with Lavanya.
We'd been together almost a year. Somewhere around Diwali I realised I didn't feel the same anymore. And I felt terrible even thinking it, because she's lovely. She did nothing wrong.
The easy thing would have been to just go quiet. Reply late, reply less, let her figure it out. A lot of people do that. I almost did.
But I asked her to meet at the park near her house. I said it straight: "I don't feel the same way anymore. It's not anything you did. I'm really sorry." She cried. I felt awful watching her.
Then the hardest part: I didn't text her that night asking if she was okay, even though I wanted to. That would've been mixed messages. I gave her space. Now we nod at each other in class, and that's fine.

qa.q: Where did Joseph and Lavanya meet to talk?
qa.a: At the park near her house.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel about ending things?
qa.a: Joseph felt guilty and awful, because Lavanya had done nothing wrong and cried when Joseph told her.

qa.q: Which choices made Joseph's breakup respectful?
qa.a: Joseph told Lavanya face to face and honestly, didn't blame her, didn't ghost, and gave her space instead of sending mixed messages.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lavanya if Joseph had simply gone quiet?
qa.a: She would have been confused and hurt, left guessing what was wrong, which would have been crueller than an honest talk.

grounding: A teen who ends a relationship feels guilty but is honest and respectful, avoids mixed messages and gives space instead of ghosting.

Leela, you asked if I ever forgave your Meenakshi Mami for the way she ended things with me in college. Oh no, beta, not her. Before her, there was a girl called Anita. I was seventeen.
Anita dropped me for my best friend. Told half the college I was boring. For months I was angry. I rehearsed speeches. I imagined her regretting it. I'd go to sleep angry and wake up angry.
Then one evening in the bus, I noticed I was clenching my jaw again, over something from six months back. I was so tired. That was the turning point: I thought, she's not even thinking about me, and I'm carrying this every day.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11C, Wednesday
During the first period, Samir's friend Yusuf asked to speak to me privately. He said private messages Samir had sent to his ex, Rehana, had been posted in a class group chat overnight, with mocking comments. Samir was in the washroom and wouldn't come out.
I went to him at once. He was shaking. I told him clearly that what was done to him is serious and wrong, and in no way his fault.
With his permission, Yusuf and I saved screenshots of the posts, the group name and times, before anything was deleted. I informed the principal before second period. Samir chose to call his father from my office; his father arrived within the hour.
The principal has contacted Rehana's parents and the group admin. Samir's father plans to file a complaint with the police cyber cell tomorrow. I have asked the counsellor to meet Samir this afternoon, and I will check on him before he leaves today.

qa.q: Who told the teacher about the posted messages?
qa.a: Samir's friend Yusuf.

qa.q: How was Samir feeling when the teacher found him?
qa.a: He was shaking, clearly humiliated and frightened after his private messages were shared.

qa.q: What steps made the teacher's response wise?
qa.a: Telling Samir it wasn't his fault, saving evidence, informing the principal and Samir's father the same morning, and arranging counselling.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel after reporting it?
qa.a: Yusuf probably feels worried for Samir but relieved that a trusted adult is acting quickly.

grounding: A teacher responds when a teen's private messages are shared to shame him: evidence saved, adults told, report and support arranged.

passage:
Thursday
I don't even know how to write this. Hafsa, my ex, sent screenshots of our private messages to her friends. The ones where I said I get nervous before exams and cried after Nana died. Now they're in a group of thirty people. Someone added laughing faces.
I wanted to disappear. I thought about not going back to school, ever.
But I remembered what the cyber-safety talk said: save everything first. So I took screenshots of the group, the names, the times.
Then I told Papa when he got home. He read everything, sat down next to me and said, "Chaitanya, this is not your fault. What she did is wrong, and serious." He wrote to the principal tonight. Tomorrow we're going to school together, and on Saturday we'll go to the police cyber cell to file a complaint.
I still feel sick. But I'm not holding it alone.

qa.q: How many people were in the group with the screenshots?
qa.a: Thirty people.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling after the messages were shared?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt humiliated and sick, wanting to disappear and never go back to school.

qa.q: Which steps did Chaitanya and Papa take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Saving evidence, telling Papa the same day, emailing the principal, and planning a cyber cell complaint mean adults can act and Chaitanya isn't alone.

qa.q: How does Papa respond when he reads the messages?
qa.a: Papa sits beside Chaitanya, says clearly it isn't Chaitanya's fault and that the sharing was wrong and serious, and acts that same night.

grounding: A teen whose private messages were shared to shame them saves evidence, tells a parent the same day and plans to report it.
